title: He Could Win Any Room. He Could Not Save the Business.
author: Kelly Mackin
summary: The author recounts promoting a talented, charismatic leader into a turnaround role that required unglamorous operational skills he did not possess. The leader excelled at visible work — strategy, commercial wins, room-winning — but the new role demanded invisible skills like cost structure, forecasting, and operational rigor. The author held onto him for months after recognizing the mismatch, not out of kindness, but to avoid admitting a promotion mistake. The leader's visible strengths masked his gaps twice: at the moment of promotion and again each month when good surface numbers obscured the rotting foundation. The essay argues that leaders routinely select for visible skills while the skills that hold a business together are invisible until they disappear. Decisive honesty — moving someone when a role no longer fits — serves both the person and the organization.
points: The skills that earn promotions are visible — strategy, commercial wins, charisma — while the skills that hold businesses together are invisible until they fail.
Promoting someone into a role that mismatches their strengths costs the individual, the business, and the leader who made the call.
Leaders often delay correcting a wrong placement not out of kindness but to avoid admitting their own judgment error.
A person's visible strengths can mask their hidden weaknesses twice: at the moment of promotion and throughout the tenure as surface metrics look acceptable.
Decisive honesty — acting when a role no longer fits — serves both the individual and the organization far better than delayed compassion.
quotes: I told myself I was being kind. I was not. I was protecting myself from a mistake I had made.
The skills I promoted him for are the skills anyone can see.
The skills that actually hold a business together, the rigor, the forecast that ties out, and the backlog rebuilt line by line are invisible right up until the moment they are missing.
I had promoted him for the skills that shine. Then I dropped him into a role that lived or died on the ones that never did.
His strengths hid his weaknesses from me twice. Once when I promoted him. And again, every month afterward, when the good numbers let me tell myself things were okay.
